questions.enonce_markdown: A matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is given by $\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Find $|\mathbf{M}|$, the determinant of matrix $\mathbf{M}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Expand along the first row:
$$|\mathbf{M}| = 1\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} - (-1)\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + 1\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 1\,(1 + 3) + 1\,(2 + 3) + 1\,(2 - 1) = 4 + 5 + 1 = 10.$$
$$\boxed{|\mathbf{M}| = 10}$$
Since $|\mathbf{M}| \ne 0$, $\mathbf{M}$ is invertible.

questions.enonce_markdown: For the matrix $\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$, the inverse of matrix $\mathbf{M}$. (5 marks for part (i), (a) and (b) together)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $\mathbf{M}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|\mathbf{M}|}\operatorname{adj}\mathbf{M}$, where $\operatorname{adj}\mathbf{M}$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$.

Cofactors:
- $C_{11} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 4$, $\quad C_{12} = -\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -5$, $\quad C_{13} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1$;
- $C_{21} = -\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 2$, $\quad C_{22} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$, $\quad C_{23} = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -2$;
- $C_{31} = \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = 2$, $\quad C_{32} = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = 5$, $\quad C_{33} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 3$.

Matrix of cofactors and its transpose:
$$\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -5 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname{adj}\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\mathbf{M}^{-1} = \frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.2 \\ -0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0.1 & -0.2 & 0.3 \end{pmatrix}}$$
Check: $\mathbf{M}\operatorname{adj}\mathbf{M}$ has diagonal entries $4 + 5 + 1 = 10$, $4 + 0 + 6 = 10$, $2 + 5 + 3 = 10$ and zeros elsewhere (e.g. row 1 with column 2: $2 + 0 - 2 = 0$), so $\mathbf{M}\operatorname{adj}\mathbf{M} = 10\mathbf{I}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Prove by mathematical induction that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r(3r - 1) = n^2(n + 1)$. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $P(n)$ be the statement $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r(3r - 1) = n^2(n + 1)$.

**Basis.** For $n = 1$: LHS $= 1 \times (3 - 1) = 2$ and RHS $= 1^2 \times 2 = 2$. So $P(1)$ is true. (The formula also holds for $n = 0$: both sides are $0$.)

**Inductive step.** Assume $P(k)$ is true for some integer $k \ge 1$:
$$\sum_{r=1}^{k} r(3r - 1) = k^2(k + 1).$$
Then, adding the $(k + 1)$th term,
$$\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r(3r - 1) = k^2(k + 1) + (k + 1)\big(3(k + 1) - 1\big) = (k + 1)\big[k^2 + 3k + 2\big].$$
Factorise $k^2 + 3k + 2 = (k + 1)(k + 2)$:
$$\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r(3r - 1) = (k + 1)^2(k + 2) = (k + 1)^2\big((k + 1) + 1\big),$$
which is exactly $P(k + 1)$.

**Conclusion.** $P(1)$ is true, and $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k + 1)$ for every $k \ge 1$. By the principle of mathematical induction, $P(n)$ is true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. $\blacksquare$

(Check with the standard sums: $3\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\big[(2n + 1) - 1\big] = n^2(n+1)$.)
